# FINAL ANSWER: Federico Lauria's 2014 Dissertation - Footnote 397 ## Summary of Investigation I successfully located Federico Lauria's 2014 PhD dissertation, accessed the full PDF document (409 pages), and extracted footnote 397 along with complete bibliographic details. ## 1. Dissertation Identification **Full Title:** "The Logic of the Liver": A Deontic View of the Intentionality of Desire **Institution:** University of Geneva (Université de Genève), Department of Philosophy (Département de philosophie) **Year:** 2014 **Degree:** Ph.D. (Thèse de doctorat) **Dissertation Directors:** - Julien Deonna (Professeur assistant, Université de Genève) - Gianfranco Soldati (Professeur ordinaire, Université de Fribourg) **Access:** Full PDF available at https://philarchive.org/archive/LAUQLO ## 2. Footnote 397 - Complete Text **Location:** Page 233 of the dissertation **Exact text of footnote 397:** > "Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan [6], in Silverman 2000: 174." ## 3. Context of Footnote 397 The footnote supports a quotation from Thomas Hobbes that appears in the main text: > "That which men Desire they are also sayd to Love: and to Hate those things for which they have Aversion. So that Desire, and Love, are the same thing; save that by Desire, we always signify the Absence of the Object; by Love, most commonly the Presence of the same. So also by Aversion, we signify the Absence, and by Hate, the Presence of the Object." This quote appears in Chapter 6 of Lauria's dissertation, which discusses the "Death of Desire Principle" (DODP) - the philosophical concept that desires cease to exist when one believes their content obtains. ## 4. Complete Bibliographic Details ### Primary Work Referenced: **Author:** Thomas Hobbes **Title:** Leviathan **Section:** [6] - refers to Part I, Chapter 6 of Leviathan (the chapter on the "Interior Beginnings of Voluntary Motions") **Standard Modern Edition (from Lauria's bibliography):** - Hobbes, T. (1994). *Leviathan*. Edited by E. Curley. Indianapolis: Hackett. **Original Publication:** 1651 ### Secondary Source (Anthology where the quote appears): **Editor:** Hugh J. Silverman **Title:** *Philosophy and Desire* **Series:** Continental Philosophy VII **Publisher:** Routledge **Location:** New York **Year:** 2000 **Page:** 174 **Full Citation:** Silverman, H. J. (ed.). (2000). *Philosophy and Desire*. Continental Philosophy VII. New York: Routledge. ## 5. What the Footnote References Footnote 397 references **Thomas Hobbes's *Leviathan* (1651)**, specifically Chapter 6, as reprinted in Hugh J. Silverman's 2000 anthology *Philosophy and Desire* on page 174. The passage discusses Hobbes's theory of desire, distinguishing between desire and love based on the absence or presence of their objects. This is a foundational text in the philosophy of desire and is being used by Lauria to support his discussion of the historical understanding that desires necessarily involve the absence of their objects.
